title: CADE for the Program Management Community 10.21.21

cues.text: >> I'd like to thank everyone for joining today's DAU webcast for another episode of "CADE
for the Program Management Community."
My name is Emmett Simmons.
I'm the producer for today's event.
The agenda for today -- your microphones will be muted throughout the session.
This session is being recorded, and will be posted
to dau.edu/dau-webcasts, which is listed at the bottom.
If you have any questions, please submit all your questions via the chat.
We will respond verbally to your questions towards the end.
There is a survey at the end.
We appreciate your feedback, takes a couple minutes.
If you're here for CLPs, a lot of people take a screenshot of the survey,
and there is a link inside the end of the survey if you want to copy
and paste for your CLP certificate.
And the session does qualify for up to 1.5 CLPs with supervisor approval.
And now, I'm going to turn it over to Mike Taylor to introduce our speakers.
>> Thank you, Emmett.
My name is Mike Taylor.
I'm with the business cost estimating and financial management department,
been working with the CAPEs KT [assumed spelling] for quite a while.
Matter of fact, our first offering was a lunch-and-learn back in August of 2017.
This represents the fifth iteration of working with them in collaboration to push out
or actually orient the cost and other communities.
In this case, this is a program management focus today of the capabilities of CADE,
the cost assessment data enterprise.
We first started talking about FlexFiles back in April of 2019, and we're happy to host them
on behalf of Mr. Woolsley, the president of DAU, to have the team back there,
which put on a very good presentation.
And we also opened, as they will mention --
that they will also have several follow-on training events.
We just completed a NOAS TK [assumed spelling] class
and technical virtual focus group this past week,
and I'm sure that'll be discussed a little bit.
I did want to note -- mention one other thing,
and I'm going to let the speakers introduce themselves as they go through.
But we'll have another session, and I've already promulgated it
through the contracting arms here at DAU.
That'll be on Thursday, the 4th of November for 2021,
where we'll be discussing CADE for the contracting community.
And so, if you would like to attend that session, we'll also have another session,
and Emmett and I will be hosting that.
And we'll -- just check the DAU web page for the links and so forth.
You're welcome to join at any time, and I've been working with Torri.
We are working on the second, and third, and maybe fourth quarters,
depending on how we can flesh out the schedule the next couple months.
So stay tuned, as we'll continue to schedule these events.
And without further ado, I'm going to turn it over to the team, and let them go.
Thank you again, and welcome, CADE training team.
Over.
>> Hey, good morning everyone, and thanks again, Mike and Emmett,
you know, for welcoming us back again.
It's been a great opportunity to kind of work with you all throughout the different iterations
that we've had, and we definitely love leveraging our DAU brothers and sisters
down there to utilize this platform.
So as he mentioned initially, my name is Torri Preston.
I'm the CADE training and outreach lead.
You know, I have my other team members, and as they get ready to present,
they'll introduce themselves as well.
But as you can see, what's indicated the slides currently, you know,
we've utilized several different mechanisms.
I'm just wanting to orient you with obviously the CADE website,
and we'll do a little bit of a demo later on.
So we have that listed there, and the PollEV is actually a --
is actually an engagement platform that we try to use, you know, just allow us to kind
of get a feel for, you know, who's on the line, who's engaged, you know, as well as just kind
of give us a mechanism to engage with different students throughout the presentations.
So we have a PollEV.com/ttraining456, which you'll see here displayed here shortly,
and then we'll talk a little bit later on about how you can actually access some
of these other trainings that Mike alluded to earlier with regards
to our Bridge Learning Management System.
So if anyone's on the line that's in any of our courses in the past,
pretty sure you may be relatively familiar with registering, as well as some of the courses
that are hosted in there currently.
So, at this time, we'll push to the first poll, and essentially,
this kind of gives us an idea of who do we have on the phone.
All right, so I just wanted to confirm, can everyone see this --
or Emmett and Mike, can you all see the slides currently?
>> Affirmative, over.
>> They're coming up, but you may want to go back to the URL with the poll on it.
>> Okay, sure.
We can get someone to drop it in the chat as well, but for those who did --
yep, for those who didn't have it, this is PollEv.com/ttraining456.
>> The link is on the chat, and it should be showing on the screen as well.
Over.
>> Okay, great.
Yeah, if someone just -- once we get the responses rolling in,
someone just give us a head's up that it's working well.
So -- because I know sometimes, depending on --
you know, you can either access this from your cell phone, or you can access it
from your desktop or laptop computer.
But if you do decide to access it via your cell phone, all you have to do is text ttraining456
to 22333, and it'll allow you to submit your responses there as well.
So while we get those loaded up, team, you just give us a head's
up once you guys start seeing responses.
Yeah, Torri, they seem to be coming in.
We're about 2/3 program management, about 12, 13% cost analyst, and 27% other.
So as you might expect, heavily weighted toward the PM community,
but with some supporting cost folks -- as well.
>> Awesome.
That's great, and that's kind of what we were looking for.
Awesome. So what we'll do now, we'll just push to the next poll, just so everyone can kind
of get a feel of who's on the line.
So what organization is everyone from?
So this is actually a -- should come up as a word cloud, just so people can kind
of get a feel for, you know, which type of communities
and organizations we actually have on the phone.
So we'll give that an opportunity to populate as well.
>> It's coming in.
We got a variety playing the DAU purchase fence, Navy, Air Force.
We've got Veterans' Administration.
We got Defense Contract Management Agency.
We've got Defense Logistics Agency, some folks in contracting and constructing, so Space Force,
so real good mix across the board.
Over.
>> Awesome.
That's great.
It's always good to have kind of a wide array of different organization on the line,
particularly when it comes to the soliciting feedback from the audience as well.
So, okay. So that takes us to our last question.
So we're just kind of trying to get a feel for, you know, what do you hope to gain
from today's training, and again, this is another free response question.
So hopefully, you know, us as presenters, you know, we can try our best to kind of hit some
of these items as we navigate through the training today.
They're looking for background information,
some information on FlexFile, an overview, perspective.
It's a little bit hard to tell with the word cloud if -- looking --
heavily weighted toward knowledge, information, and basically an overview of the topic.
So, we'll hit that quite well, best practices to share.
Over.
>> Awesome, definitely appreciate it.
Knowledge is power.
Way to go.
All right, so we'll get ready to push forward.
I think the next slide is going to be our presenter slide.
So as we mentioned earlier, we want to put a face with a name.
I'm the guy that's in the middle, Torri Preston, and as a team, kind of introduce --
that was Peter [assumed spelling] who was speaking earlier as well.
Ryan Sokely, Wayne Query, Zach Cole, and Jack Titus [assumed spellings] kind
of round out the remainder of our team.
Again, you know, everyone here has kind of spent, you know,
some pretty extensive time leveraging our relationship
with DAU to kind of keep things going.
So it's always been a great experience working with those guys, across the board.
All right, so with regards to what we want to cover today, you know,
obviously the intent behind this is try to help the program office community kind
of understand the benefits of CSDR reporting, as well as try to navigate
through the actual CSDR reporting process.
You know, as well as kind of understanding what your actual roles are, and the different steps,
as well as, you know, your role in the cost working group integrated product team, CWIPT.
As well as understanding, you know, what insight you can kind of gain from some
of the different CADE data to kind of make, you know, your jobs a lot easier,
as well as the analysis that you are conducting a little more easier to facilitate.
So moving to the next slide -- and we're going to send this out.
We'll get the participants list, and this is also on the CADE public site.
But essentially, the CSDR cheat sheet is what we've been calling it, and it kind of lays out,
you know, the CDR requirement matrix, as well as what some of these thresholds are
that you may see in the various OSD-CAPE policy guidance.
So it's just something to keep in your hip pocket.
You know, post it on your cube, or your desk, you know, just to have that in hand.
So when those questions come up, you know, you have a quick reference guide with regards
to how some of these CSDR deliverables and what the thresholds associated with them are.
All right, so essentially, you know, as a program manager,
you know, why should you care, right?
So that takes us to our opening slides.
So obviously, there's a -- you know, a wide array of, you know,
value that the program management community can get, you know, particularly when it comes to,
you know, generating the -- or using the CSDR either to generate, you know,
what your cost values are going to be in the various acquisition documents.
And, you know, if you're a data person, right, you know,
65% of those acquisition documents require some degree of cost information, you know,
whether that's in the milestones, or phase information requirements, or, you know,
any type of wide array of documents.
You know, there is some level of cost reporting that's associated with it.
And, you know, for all the cost analysis on the room, they can definitely attest to the --
you know, the necessity of having these documents, and why they're important.
All right, so what exactly is the -- you know, the Cost and Software Data Reporting, right?
So, again, the CSDR -- you know, it was enacted, you know, on one of the major defense contracts,
you know, for over 30 years now, and it's the primary mechanism that the DoD uses
for collecting actual cost, as well as software resources and related business efforts
that actually are incurred, you know, during the development or production of,
you know, the various defense systems.
So per the -- you know, the DoD 5000.73, you know, CSDR is kind of consists
of a few distinct elements, right?
So as indicated on the sheet, you have your contractor cost data reporting,
and your software resource data reporting, SRDRs.
And again, you know, CCDRs, you know, are the DoD's primary mechanism for, you know,
essentially systematically collecting data on development, production,
and sustainment costs for various contracts.
And again, you know, while the SRDR's basically a supplement, you know, to the CCDR,
with some of the software metrics, it is designed to kind
of help provide a better understanding of, you know,
improving the estimating of software-intensive programs.
So, you know, while, you know, CSDRs are, you know, a good idea for the most part, you know,
there's several different things that you kind of want to think about.
First and foremost, you know, with the publication of the 2017 NDAA,
CSDRs are generally required on all programs with a life cycle cost that's greater
than 100 million, and for contracts that exceed that $50 million threshold.
As well as, you know, if you think about software reporting, you know,
it's required for major contracts and subcontracts, you know,
that have that projected value of software -- greater than that $20 million threshold.
So we always try to have a couple of the key things that we need,
and this slide is essentially designed to help you understand, hey, you know,
your CCRs and your SRDRs are kind of what help us generate that CSDR cost report.
And again, we'll continue to reference the CDRIL [phonetic] matrix kind
of throughout the presentation, but again, we'll be sure to make that available.
And you can also pull that down from the CADE public website.
All right, so we want to talk through some of the types of CSDRs on the next slide.
You know, we also want to try to understand -- so we have --
we'll just kind of orient ourselves this way.
So if you think through the statutory and kind of regulatory mandates, you know,
of the costs of software data reporting, you know, there are several different reports
that we kind of want to work through.
So if you're a kind of chart person like we me,
we can just kind of orient ourselves in the center.
So we'll start with, you know, the CSDR plan, which is actually not a type of CSDR,
but kind of the rules of the road that kind of lays the initial framework for, you know,
the work breakdown structure, and kind of helps us ensure that the reporting requirements
and the structure, you know, are properly defined, whether it's the cost, software,
and the technical data reporting that's given for, you know, the contracts and the contractor.
You know, there are there types of kind of plans.
So you have the program plan, which kind of outlines the scope of work
for a specific program, the contract plan, you know, outlining your reporting requirements
for whoever that prime contractor is.
And then you have the subcontractor plan
that outlines what requirements are actually flowed down to the subcontractor.
So we'll start with the chart, kind of moving clockwise with the contractor cost data report.
So again, the cost in our report, or the FlexFile that Mike mentioned earlier --
you know, this is primarily requirement for reporting, you know, your actual cost and hours,
you know, according to the contract line item number, or the CLIN,
the company's rate structure, as well as that product-oriented work breakdown structure.
A couple key things about the FlexFile -- it's definitely time -- by month.
It provides insight at what us at the DCARC are calling the account level,
where the contractor actually incurs cost to their system.
You know, ultimately, this level will be determined by the contractor,
but it's most likely going to take the shape of, you know, either a work package,
a control account, a charge number, or some type of similar element.
So moving down to the quantity report --
so because the FlexFile is kind of primarily a financial report, it did necessitate the need
for us to kind of have a separate report that captures, you know,
that relevant quantity information.
So, you know, the quantity report essentially ties together the necessary quantity information
to the FlexFile.
So the -- you know, the quantities are tagged to the WBS [phonetic], you know, order lots,
and the end items, which kind of makes it possible to make those discrete ties that we try
to look for when the various analysts are doing their analysis.
As we continue down forward, it takes us to the contract business data report, or the 1921-3.
So essentially, you know, this system is designed for collecting that direct
and indirect cost in our employee data at the business center level, and it's just kind
of based on the terms of whatever the contractor's own proposed categories are.
And, you know, the report also includes, you know, that summary-level capacity, labor,
and sales data, and is essentially designed to kind of help assist with the development of,
you know, those independent government cost estimates, as well as kind of support,
from a program office perspective, that cost and price analyses that are associated
with some of these contract negotiations.
You know, it does kind of provide a basis for, you know,
the assessment of a contractor's overhead, cost data kind of during, you know,
the progress of the contract as well.
Okay. So we'll shift over to going through some of the technical reports.
So if you think about -- we'll start in the top left.
So we'll walk through the maintenance and repair report.
So essentially, it's kind of used by contractors to submit, you know,
that maintenance event data, you know, which is, you know, related to each maintenance event,
you know, whether it's specific to a system being repaired, you know,
the location where that repair activity took place, you know, the reason for the failure,
as well as, you know, other maintenance-related data as well.
The technical report is essentially providing a mechanism for us to kind
of systematically capture that tech data on contracts.
It also creates a common technical data vocabulary, which essentially defines some
of those coarse sets that are needed in the parameters.
It also kind of leverages other technical data on the contract to kind of help us kind
of review, you know, whether it's the program technical baseline,
and kind of describe the technical parameters that are required
to develop a program life cycle cost estimate.
So, again, lots of relatively good information in the technical reports.
If you had an opportunity to attend one of the webinar series that we've hosted previously,
it kind of goes into the technical data report in a little bit of granular detail,
just to kind of go through some of the benefits of that report as well.
And then, lastly, in the middle here, we have the software resource data report, or SRDRs.
So essentially, you know, it provides the insight on the size, schedule,
and effort on data for software development.
And as we mentioned earlier, you know, the software development effort, you know --
that $20 million threshold, that's when we kind of want to get
into the actual reporting of the SRDRs.
So one of the things we want to note here is that, you know, an SRDR is never collected,
you know, without a corresponding CCDR, so just something to keep
in your mind or in your hip pocket as well.
All right.
So that'll take us down to some of the types of the legacy CCDRs.
As you can see, you know, a lot of these reports are relatively similar
to what we described earlier, but the FlexFile just kind of gives us the ability
to capture all these in -- you know, in a more efficient manner.
But with that being said -- so if you do find yourself kind of conducting some
of that legacy reporting, as you can see indicated here,
we'll start with the contract work breakdown structure.
So similar to what we mentioned earlier, you know, essentially,
documents the contractor's planned approach for kind of performing the contract scope of work,
as well as kind of describing the end item that's actually being developed or procured.
So we'll move over to the cost data summary report, or the 1921.
So essentially, you know, we have our summary cost data for, you know,
all the elements that are approved on that CSDR plan that we just mentioned.
Again, it does -- similar to the FlexFile, you know, it contains the cost
for both cost-to-date, at completion.
It is broken out by non-recurring and recurring, and it also kind of contains some
of that quantity information that we alluded to earlier.
All right, so the 1921-1, or the function cost-hour report --
again, that kind of breaks out the cost and hours out into, you know,
those functional labor categories, you know, engineering, manufacturing,
quality control, as well as tooling.
And kind of one of the big key takeaways is that, you know, it essentially enables,
you know, you from the program office perspective to conduct that labor
versus material analysis, you know, your hours versus dollars,
engineering versus manufacturing, as well as kind of a wide array of different things
when it comes to dealing with the direct labor hours and the overhead dollars associated
with those various functional categories.
All right.
And as far as our 1921-5, again, so the 1921-5 sustainment report is kind
of broken out the same way as the 1921-1.
However, except the functional categories are aligned towards,
you know, sustainment-type activities.
You know, the functional labor categories of, you know, engineering, program management,
maintenance, and support maintenance, you know, for a given effort.
And then, lastly, we have our progress curve report, or our 1921-2.
So again, you know, you have your lot or unit reporting of, you know, some of those direct,
recurring costs to date, you know, for specific hardware elements.
You know, one of the key things with regards to the 1921-2 is that, you know, that by unit lot
and sublot reporting will kind of help facilitate
that good old learning curve analysis.
So I know in our previous trainings, specifically for CADE 101, you know,
that question was brought up a few times.
You know, hey, what are we doing with the 1921-2, and it's kind of one
of those key components to facilitating the learning curve analysis.
All right, so we kind of walked through, you know, what some of these reports are,
big picture level, but, okay, what's in it for the program office, and why should you comply?
Well, first and foremost, as indicated on the slide, it is the law, but again, you know,
one of the things you have to think about is kind of how these things arise, right?
So, you know, obviously with the Weapons System Acquisition Reform Act back in 2009, you know,
it essentially, you know, imbued the Office of -- the OSD-CAPE office, you know,
with the responsibility of performing, you know, cost estimates and analysis for, you know,
the various acquisition programs.
So as we mentioned previously, you know, when the 2017 NDAA was inserted, you know,
it essentially requires cost data collection from acquisition programs over $100 million.
And, you know, obviously, these are going to be in accordance with the policies and procedures
that you have on the OSD-CAPE public website.
But we just kind of want to walk you through just a quick color chart of kind
of how these things come into play.
So for those of you who know me, you know, I'm a Marine by trade, and obviously,
I can tell you Marines love colors.
So if you're looking at this chart, everything that's in yellow essentially kind
of describes the documents that actually mandate the reporting.
Everything that's green essentially highlights, you know, when you need to report, you know,
the associated thresholds, policies associated with those, the details,
and kind of how to fill out the form.
Everything in orange is essentially the parameters for how you should actually --
or how you need to report, you know, the details on schedules, and then, you know,
the MIL STDs that are associated with that.
And everything down there in blue kind of highlights, you know,
the details of what you're actually reporting.
So that's a quick summary, but if we go back, starting with the DFARS,
essentially the DFARS has three main clauses that, you know, you kind of want to think
about when it comes to the contract.
So first, you know, all costs must reflect, you know, the actual transactional cost,
you know, to the maximum extent possible.
You know, secondly, you know, we want to make sure the contracts are actually discussing
that approach that they're using to execute CSDR reporting in their proposal.
And then lastly, you know, we'll talk a little bit about the post-award conference,
and the significance when it comes to, you know,
walking through the intent behind what the actual reporting,
and the concerns that the contractors may have in executing the reports.
So if we think about the 5000.02, this kind of states the thresholds
and the interpretation for, you know, what's going to be considered on a contract.
You know, what's necessary for requesting a waiver, and things of that nature.
You know, waivers are kind of a rare occurrence, for lack of better words, but we've kind of got
to have, you know, parameters in place in the event that a waiver is necessary.
As far as the 5000.73, you know, it essentially is going
to define the CSDR reporting thresholds that we alluded to earlier.
The 5000.04, you know, is going to outline the process for the CSDR planning and execution,
which we'll get into here in a little bit.
And then we talked through the MIL STD 881, which essentially is going
to guide the structures that we use.
It's also going to kind of provide that basis of the WS, you know, and also an extension
of how we kind of standardize the WBS below the levels of three and four.
And essentially, you know, the remaining documents listed here, as we mentioned,
are just how we actually implement the process.
So, as we alluded to earlier, you know, we have several references that are available,
that go into, you know, extreme detail, in terms of how these reports look,
how they can be manipulated, and what you actually need
in order to populate these forms as well.
>> Torri, Mike.
I think Peter answered a question, but Brian Schultz [assumed spelling] puts a question.
Is this only for FAR-based contracts only, cost incentive-type contracts, and if so,
how do we collect data on commercial companies for analysis?
Over. I think you alluded to it, but I wanted to go straight at the jump with that question.
Over.
>> Yeah, Torri, just so that -- to summarize what I put in the chat.
It's generally for all contract types, regardless.
So it's not just cost and incentive types.
It includes fixed-price contracts.
So Brian used the term "commercial companies."
If it's truly a commercial item, we don't generally do CSDR, but there's plenty
of commercial companies, like a Microsoft or like a Cerner, that are doing --
you know, providing goods and services to the department.
And we generally would do CSDR in those, and there's ways to tailor that.
So I put a reference in to a presentation from yesterday that we can share.
So if anybody's interested in that, you can put your e-mail in the chat.
Or if Mike has that through the registration,
then we'd be happy to send that up as a follow-up.
Also, any kind of contracting details like that, as Torri mentioned, we'll be doing --
and I think Mike mentioned as well --
we will be doing another session in a couple weeks that'll focus a little bit more
on the contracting community.
We may get more into that -- those details.
Over.
>> Great, thank you, Peter.
We just got a quick question on OTAs also.
Does it apply there?
Over.
>> Yes, it can apply to OTAs.
I know that the DAU contracting fan is very broad,
so we can't swear to answer every little wedge in that fan.
But yeah, generally speaking, as Torri said, it would apply once you're
over the dollar value threshold, unless you get a waiver for most,
if not all of those contract types.
>> Thank you, Peter.
Over.
>> Awesome.
So that brings us to the last slide of this initial portion of the brief.
It's kind of -- it's talking to some of the concerns and mitigation, right?
So obviously, you know, there are going to be a certain level of burdens
that are associated with, you know, the individual program offices, you know,
and their production contractors.
But I think the benefits of capturing, you know,
this high-quality cot data will ultimately improve the decision-making process, you know,
for all the future programs, right?
And I think it's kind of worth the cost, for lack of better words.
You know, for example, you know, developing the CSDR plans -- you know, they're required by law,
and obviously, you know, it's a programmatic reporting responsibility.
That's no different than kind of any of the other technical
and engineering reporting requirements that a program office would kind of have,
when it comes to managing their program.
And, you know, like other milestones and other programmatic reporting, you know,
the government staff already kind of has ready access to, you know, the DAU-provided training,
as well as some of the training that we provide to kind of help enable them to perform
and execute when it comes to this reporting.
And, you know, the same thing kind of holds true to, you know, when it comes to staffing,
and kind of drafting the final program, and the contract CSDR plans.
You know, the schedule to CSDR plans, you know --
its review and approval is no more burdensome than, you know, the actual acquisition artifacts
that are needed to facilitate the milestone reviews, right?
So I think one of the greatest challenges for, you know, the CSDR reporting will kind of be --
come from the contractors, right?
Because obviously, they want to kind of minimize, you know,
the cost that they're incurring for the actual cost reporting.
So, you know, regardless of, you know, what their motivation level would be, you know,
their internal systems, you know, aren't necessarily equipped
to facilitate capturing some of this effort data,
or whether they just don't want to do it, right?
I just think, you know, the continuous engagement with -- from a program office level,
you know, the continuous engagement with the contractors, you know, early on, you know,
about what the actual requirements are, and kind of prepping the battlefield so that, you know,
it's that much easier when that time comes.
So again, over the time, you know, we've kind of seen, you know,
various arguments with regards to, you know,
contractors pushing back against the program offices.
You know, why do we have to report this way, this, that, and the third,
but our more successful program managers and program offices have been able
to facilitate a good relationship with their reporting contractors,
let them know what the requirements are early on, particularly for the prime,
and kind of what's getting flowed down to the subcontractors as well.
And I think that relationship has essentially allowed, you know,
us to facilitate what we do here at CAPE, right?
Having, you know, cost and software data reporting that we use to kind of pay it forward
to the analysts that are coming down the line, right?
So the best benefit I can say is, you know, your astute management as a program office now,
you know, will facilitate, you know, analyst X, you know, X many years down the line
when it comes to him doing -- him or her doing their actual cost analysis.
So that kind of wraps up this initial portion, and then we'll kind of transition
over to our next team member to take us through some of the CWIPT stuff.
>> All right, can you guys hear me out there?
>> Yep, we got you loud and clear.
>> Perfect, thanks.
Hi, everybody.
So I'm Ryan Sokely.
I've been a member of the CADE training team for almost a year now,
primarily managing online courses, but also getting involved
in live trainings here and there.
And I"m going to be going through the process of CSDR development and execution,
talking about the role of program managers, but then also the role of various members
of the acquisition community in enabling that process to run smoothly.
So, Jack, if you can -- perfect.
Let me wait until the slide pops up.
Great. So the development and evaluation of CSDRs is a major process that involves members
from all different sides of the acquisition community,
and it all starts with the DoD program management offices, which is most of you.
The PMO and contracting agency are responsible for notifying OSD CAPE and the CWIPT.
We'll explain what that is in a second --
notifying them of upcoming contracts or actions requiring CSDRs.
The PMO also works with other members of the CWIPT to prepare CSDR plans and plan revisions,
to incorporate approved CSDR plan into a solicitation, like an RFP,
and to ensure that CSDRs are submitted in a timely manner pursuant to approved CSDR plans.
The cost working group integrated product team is the second group there.
